name: Flight carbon footprint
seoTitle: Flight carbon footprint Calculator — Formula, Units & Example
seoDesc: Flight carbon footprint: work out seat occupancy from the duration of a flight and the yearly allowance. A free ecology calculator with the formula, units…
summary: Supply the duration of a flight and the yearly allowance and the Flight carbon footprint calculator solves for seat occupancy. That makes it useful for a footprint, a resource or an environmental change you want to size up. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Flight carbon footprint calculator work?
sections.html:
The Flight carbon footprint calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports seat occupancy in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the flight); then you type in the duration of a flight and the yearly allowance.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A measured quantity, entered by default in hours. The unit chip switches it to any of the 27 supported units.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as one-way and return. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in percent. The unit chip switches it to any of the 6 supported units.

1 field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Flight carbon footprint calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Seat occupancy=180 × flight × duration of a flight ÷ CO₂ emissions
CO₂ emissions=2500 × yearly allowance

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Duration of a flight = 10 hrs, Flight set to One-way, Seat occupancy = 10 % and CO₂ emissions = 10 kg. Working through the relationship above gives Yearly allowance = 0.4 %.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Yearly allowance = 0.4 % should be roughly the size you expected from Duration of a flight = 10 hrs and Flight set to One-way.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in percent, and convertible to any of the 6 units on that chip.
  • Shown in kilograms, and convertible to any of the 29 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Time, opening in hours
  • %, opening in percent
  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • %, opening in percent

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Flight carbon footprint calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Sizing an environmental impact in familiar units
  • Comparing two options on the same basis
  • Putting a headline figure into context
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the duration of a flight and the yearly allowance — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the Flight carbon footprint calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns seat occupancy, derived from the duration of a flight and the yearly allowance. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Flight carbon footprint calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the duration of a flight and the yearly allowance, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter duration of a flight in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Duration of a flight opens in hours and the chip beside it offers 27 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Yearly allowance = 0.4 %. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Flight carbon footprint calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
